newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deputies complain about absent Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Russian deputies complain about absent Yeltsin.

text.p: Russian lawmakers, complaining at their ailing president's long absence from the corridors of power, began looking at ways to force him out of office on Tuesday, but admitted they were unlikely to succeed.

The speaker of the State Duma lower house, communist Gennady Seleznyov, said constitutional provisions to oust a head of state on health grounds were "very hazy" and forecast a proposal to do so from parliament's security committee would fail.
The motion will be discussed by the Duma's legal department and then by party groups.

"It means Yeltsin will be dismissed," communist deputy Viktor Ilyukhin told reporters. In fact there is virtually no chance of that, although the discussions could throw some light on the constitutional position on presidential illness.
Yeltsin, incapacitated first with heart problems and now with pneumonia, has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since he won a second term in office on July 3.

He is in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital and a Kremlin spokeswoman said doctors would issue a medical bulletin after they meet on Tuesday afternoon. The Kremlin has given no sign of when Yeltsin, 65, might leave hospital.

Doctors have insisted the pneumonia has nothing to do with Yeltsin's heart bypass operation on November 5. But it has been a political blow to the president and creates the risk of another power vacuum in Russia.

Yeltsin, clearly seeking to reassure Russians that he was keeping a close eye on affairs of state, on Monday proposed holding referendums in Russia and Belarus on whether the two Slav former Soviet republics should merge.
Gennady Zyuganov, whose Communist Party is the largest single party in the Duma, said the suggestion was poorly timed.
"I find this suggestion rather strange. As soon as the internal situation in the country gets worse, it becomes acceptable to throw in new ideas," Zyuganov said.
Alexander Lebed, ousted Russian security chief, said Yeltsin's initiative was a "political trick".

"The idea itself is a good one, but considering the timing of the announcement, it looks like another attempt to divert Russian society's attention away from vital internal state problems," Lebed told Interfax news agency.
"The Belarussian card, which has become fashionable in recent times, has been played again."
Analysts expressed doubt over how long Yeltsin would be able to hold the advantage he may have won with his Belarus proposal.

"I believe this is a card in the ongoing poker match between East and West over NATO enlargement," said one Western expert based in Moscow, referring to Moscow's fierce opposition to the Western defence alliance's expansion plans.

Sergei Shakhrai, deputy head of the Kremlin administration, said on Monday that a merger between the two countries' could be the best response to any NATO expansion move, sending the message, "If you go East, we'll go West".
But economists said a merger could be costly for Russia at a time of tough economic problems at home.
"You have a weak cousin being absorbed by a country that doesn't have the resources to look after itself," said Gavin Rankin, director of research at Troika-Dialog bank in Moscow.

Russia's economic problems include massive wage delays affecting millions of workers. Teachers across the country are on strike because they have not been paid. Unions say more than three million children are affected.

Russia won praise from the IMF last year for bringing inflation down, but structural reforms have been slow, stalled in the first half by costly promises during Yeltsin's re-election campaign and in the second half by his illness.

Yet reforms have barely begun in Belarus where the economy is in a much sorrier state. An IMF delegation arrived in Moscow on Tuesday to discuss the state of the Russian economy. No IMF talks are planned in Minsk.
